source.title: Unique Properties of Wide Minima in Deep Networks

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the paper and supplementary material. The title in the paper text differs slightly from the catalog title; no other document problem noted.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether sharpness relates to generalization and argues that common sharpness measures are not directly tied to generalization; its own experiments compare sharp and flat solutions but measure denoising loss, not the train–test gap in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports Hessian sharpness, intermediate gains, train loss, and validation loss. Its generalization discussion is an argument, not a measured test of any listed version’s train–test gap, architecture advantage, optimizer generalization difference, or memorization effect. Rows capture the measured properties relevant to V7; no claim-version labels are warranted because the experiments do not measure the generalization gap.
record.test_reason: The study characterizes unnormalized Hessian sharpness and intermediate gains in linear regression and fully connected MNIST denoising networks. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure in a convolutional family or any other listed version. Its argument about sharpness and generalization concerns a different sharpness definition and model setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors prove restrained intermediate amplification and singular-vector coupling for flattest minima in linear networks with quadratic loss, and illustrate related behavior in nonlinear denoising networks. They distinguish optimizer-stability sharpness from generalization measures; they do not demonstrate failure of magnitude-aware sharpness to track generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Studies flatness defined by maximal Hessian eigenvalue and intermediate gains in linear regression theory and MNIST denoising experiments; it does not reproduce the versions’ generalization-gap, width, or memorization protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization, optimizer, step size, and depth change measured sharpness and intermediate gains; identity versus He initialization changes sharpness and convergence behavior. The experiment also compares SGD with large step size and Adam with small step size.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger step sizes and identity initialization yield flatter Hessian minima; the lowest measured sharpness increases roughly linearly with depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth, initialization and step size affect unnormalized Hessian sharpness in fully connected MNIST denoising networks.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD produces smaller intermediate gains and lower Hessian sharpness than Adam in the tested six-layer denoising setup.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Flatter denoising solutions have more restrained intermediate signal amplification under the tested optimizer settings.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD has lower training and validation loss than Adam; the approximate validation-minus-training loss gaps are 0.0001 and 0.0006, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The reported SGD recipe outperforms the reported Adam recipe on MNIST denoising; this comparison does not establish the effect of limited optimizer tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 2 argues that linear networks can implement different functions with identical local loss landscapes when inputs occupy a lower-dimensional subspace.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unnormalized Hessian sharpness need not distinguish functions with different generalization behavior in this linear-regression setting.

fits_no_version.finding: All 16 tested flat–sharp solution pairs reverse their apparent sharpness ordering along the connecting line.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss interpolation between two minima can misrepresent their ordering by maximal Hessian eigenvalue.

record.problems: The experiments concern MNIST denoising rather than the classification and train–test error settings in the claim versions. The key gain comparisons are plotted without numeric values in the text. Four random initializations are used for the optimizer comparison; no direct generalization-gap analysis is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible rows omitted; cited prior work and generalization assertions without this study's own outcome were not entered as results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD generalization on classification or language benchmarks under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out classifier error.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance versus generalization gaps within a convolutional family, including ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The absence of an explicit gap analysis is not itself decisive: Table S1 allows approximate loss gaps to be calculated. The decisive mismatch is the sharpness definition, architecture and task. The study's own linear argument does not challenge V7's narrower correlational claim.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width beyond interpolation threshold and test error.

The paper discusses sharpness and generalization conceptually, and measures Hessian sharpness and validation loss, but does not measure the train–test generalization gap or the magnitude-aware perturbation measure in this version.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: fully connected ReLU networks trained with identity initialization
rows.operation_detail: Measured top Hessian eigenvalue for runs across depths and step sizes; figure tiles encode sharpness.
rows.note: Text states larger step sizes lead to flatter minima and maximal convergent step size behaves as 1/m; exact tile values are figure-only. This does not measure test error or a train–test gap.
rows.check: Hessian eigenvalues measure sharpness, without the magnitude-aware perturbations or generalization-gap comparison required by V7.

rows.subject: fully connected ReLU networks trained with identity initialization
rows.operation_detail: Plotted the lowest measured sharpness at each network depth.
rows.measure: Lowest measured top Hessian eigenvalue versus number of layers
rows.note: Authors state flattest minima get sharper as depth increases, roughly linearly. Not a test-error measure.
rows.check: This is the lowest measured sharpness selected from the step-size sweep at each depth, not a demonstrated global minimum of sharpness. It measures no listed version.

rows.subject: fully connected ReLU networks trained with He initialization
rows.operation_detail: Measured top Hessian eigenvalue across depths and step sizes.
rows.note: Text says random initialization yields sharper minima and tolerates smaller maximal step sizes than identity initialization. Exact values are figure-only.
rows.check: The initialization comparison measures unnormalized Hessian sharpness and convergence, not a listed generalization effect.

rows.subject: 18-layer fully connected ReLU network, identity initialization
rows.size_stated: 18 layers; over 600,000 × m parameters stated for the experiment family
rows.operation_detail: Compared training-loss progression for identity and random initializations.
rows.note: Text says identity initialization converges rapidly at an early stage while random initialization decreases only at later iterations; no numeric values.
rows.check: Training-loss progression measures convergence speed, not held-out generalization.

rows.subject: six-layer fully connected ReLU network trained with SGD
rows.size_stated: over 600,000 × m parameters stated for the experiment family
rows.operation_detail: Estimated maximal intermediate gain over 100 random input initializations and measured top Hessian eigenvalue.
rows.measure: Intermediate gains by layer and Hessian sharpness
rows.note: Text reports SGD minima had significantly smaller top Hessian eigenvalue, roughly 6×, and gains were more restrained than for Adam. This is not a measured generalization gap.
rows.check: Intermediate gains and unnormalized Hessian sharpness do not measure V7. Separate these measures if retaining the row; Table S1 supplies SGD sharpness of 1.76 ± 0.00943.

rows.measure: Intermediate gains by layer and Hessian sharpness
rows.baseline: SGD with large step size; figure-only
rows.note: Text says Adam reached sharper minima with high intermediate gains compared with SGD; exact gains are figure-only.

rows.subject: fully connected ReLU networks trained with SGD and Adam
rows.operation_detail: Compared train loss, validation loss, and top Hessian eigenvalue across four random initializations per method.
rows.note: The table reports aggregate results for the two methods. Denoising validation loss is not the generalization-gap measure named by the versions.
rows.check: Split the two optimizers and three measures into separate rows. The values are correctly transcribed. Train and validation losses do permit approximate loss-gap calculation: 0.0001 for SGD and 0.0006 for Adam. However, these fully connected denoising results do not test V7's specified measure and architecture or V4's classification/language benchmarks. Tuning scope is also unspecified.
